cards.heading: Tail latency histograms: definition
cards.question: What is a tail latency histogram, and why is it preferred over recording averages?
cards.answer: Request counts bucketed by latency, with boundaries spaced roughly exponentially, instead of raw latencies or means — so a slow tail shows up as its own visible population instead of being absorbed into a mean that describes no request anyone actually made.

cards.heading: Why averages hide the tail
cards.question: If a service averages 100ms and 1% of requests take five seconds, what does that imply about the other 99% of requests?
cards.answer: The remaining 99% must run about twice as fast as the average — believing most requests sit near the mean, without a measured distribution, is simply hope.

cards.heading: Tail latency compounds across fan-out
cards.question: Why is tail latency a system property rather than a per-service curiosity?
cards.answer: When a page is assembled from several backends, one backend's 99th percentile becomes the frontend's median.

cards.heading: Why bucketing is cheap
cards.question: Why does bucket-based latency collection cost the same regardless of request rate?
cards.answer: Each request only increments a counter in its bucket, rather than recording and storing an individual latency value.

cards.heading: Choosing measurement resolution per signal
cards.question: What is the governing rule for choosing measurement resolution, according to this concept?
cards.answer: Pick resolution per signal against what the target actually requires — e.g. minute-resolution CPU averages hide the spikes that drive tail latency, but probing a three-nines service more than once or twice a minute buys nothing.
